claim: Perceptual choices depend not only on the current sensory input but also on the behavioral context, such as the history of one's own choices.
source: Perceptual choices depend not only on the current sensory input but also on the behavioral context, such as the history of one's own choices.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general premise of the study.

claim: In models of decision formation, it is commonly assumed that choice history shifts the starting point of accumulation toward the bound reflecting the previous choice.
source: In models of decision formation, it is commonly assumed that choice history shifts the starting point of accumulation toward the bound reflecting the previous choice.
evidence: This is stated as a common assumption in existing models, referencing established theoretical frameworks.

claim: Individual history biases in overt behavior were consistently explained by a history-dependent change in the evidence accumulation, rather than in its starting point.
source: Across multiple task protocols and sensory modalities, individual history biases in overt behavior were consistently explained by a history-dependent change in the evidence accumulation, rather than in its starting point.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by model fitting results across six datasets.

claim: Choice history signals bias the interpretation of current sensory input, akin to shifting endogenous attention toward (or away from) the previously selected interpretation.
source: Choice history signals thus seem to bias the interpretation of current sensory input, akin to shifting endogenous attention toward (or away from) the previously selected interpretation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the main finding, drawing on inference about the mechanism.

claim: Decisions are not isolated events, but are embedded in a sequence of choices.
source: Decisions are not isolated events, but are embedded in a sequence of choices.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established knowledge in decision-making research.

claim: Choices, or their outcomes (e.g. rewards), exert a large influence on subsequent decisions (Sutton and Barto, 1998; Sugrue et al., 2004).
source: Choices, or their outcomes (e.g. rewards), exert a large influence on subsequent decisions (Sutton and Barto, 1998; Sugrue et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Perceptual decisions are strongly influenced by experimental history: whether or not previous choices led to positive outcomes (Rabbitt and Rodgers, 1977; Dutilh et al., 2012), the confidence in them (Desender et al., 2018), and the content of the previous choice (i.e. which stimulus category was selected; Akaishi et al., 2014; Fründ et al., 2014; Urai et al., 2017).
source: Yet, perceptual decisions are strongly influenced by experimental history: whether or not previous choices led to positive outcomes (Rabbitt and Rodgers, 1977; Dutilh et al., 2012), the confidence in them (Desender et al., 2018), and the content of the previous choice (i.e. which stimulus category was selected; Akaishi et al., 2014; Fründ et al., 2014; Urai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Choice history biases are prevalent in human (Fründ et al., 2014; Urai et al., 2017), monkey (Gold et al., 2008) and rodent (Busse et al., 2011; Odoemene et al., 2018) perceptual decision-making.
source: Choice history biases are prevalent in human (Fründ et al., 2014; Urai et al., 2017), monkey (Gold et al., 2008) and rodent (Busse et al., 2011; Odoemene et al., 2018) perceptual decision-making.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research across multiple species.

claim: Choice history biases hold even for environments lacking any correlations between stimuli presented on successive trials – the standard in psychophysical laboratory experiments.
source: Remarkably, this holds even for environments lacking any correlations between stimuli presented on successive trials – the standard in psychophysical laboratory experiments.
evidence: This is stated as a notable observation about choice history biases, supported by the experimental design of the studies cited.

claim: Choice history biases vary substantially across individuals (Abrahamyan et al., 2016; Urai et al., 2017).
source: Choice history biases vary substantially across individuals (Abrahamyan et al., 2016; Urai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neural signals reflecting previous choices have been found across the sensorimotor pathways of the cerebral cortex, from sensory to associative and motor regions (Gold et al., 2008; de Lange et al., 2013; Akaishi et al., 2014; Pape and Siegel, 2016; Purcell and Kiani, 2016a; St John-Saaltink et al., 2016; Thura et al., 2017; Hwang et al., 2017; Scott et al., 2017).
source: Neural signals reflecting previous choices have been found across the sensorimotor pathways of the cerebral cortex, from sensory to associative and motor regions (Gold et al., 2008; de Lange et al., 2013; Akaishi et al., 2014; Pape and Siegel, 2016; Purcell and Kiani, 2016a; St John-Saaltink et al., 2016; Thura et al., 2017; Hwang et al., 2017; Scott et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: Current models of perceptual decision-making posit the temporal accumulation of sensory evidence, resulting in an internal decision variable that grows with time (Bogacz et al., 2006; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008; Brody and Hanks, 2016).
source: Current models of perceptual decision-making posit the temporal accumulation of sensory evidence, resulting in an internal decision variable that grows with time (Bogacz et al., 2006; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008; Brody and Hanks, 2016).
evidence: This claim describes the theoretical framework of accumulation-to-bound models, supported by citations.

claim: When the decision variable reaches one of two decision bounds, a choice is made and the corresponding motor response is initiated.
source: When this decision variable reaches one of two decision bounds, a choice is made and the corresponding motor response is initiated.
evidence: This is a description of the accumulation-to-bound model framework.

claim: A bias can arise in two ways: (i) by shifting the starting point of accumulation toward one of the bounds or (ii) by selectively changing the rate at which evidence for one versus the other choice alternative is accumulated.
source: In this framework, a bias can arise in two ways: (i) by shifting the starting point of accumulation toward one of the bounds or (ii) by selectively changing the rate at which evidence for one versus the other choice alternative is accumulated.
evidence: This describes the two mechanisms of bias within the DDM framework, as illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The starting point shift can be thought of as adding an offset to the perceptual interpretation of the current sensory evidence.
source: The starting point shift can be thought of as adding an offset to the perceptual interpretation of the current sensory evidence.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the starting point bias mechanism.

claim: The evidence accumulation bias corresponds to biasing that perceptual interpretation toward one of the two stimulus categories.
source: By contrast, the evidence accumulation bias corresponds to biasing that perceptual interpretation toward one of the two stimulus categories.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the drift bias mechanism.

claim: Previous theoretical accounts have postulated a shift in the starting point of the decision variables toward the bound of the previous choice (Yu and Cohen, 2008; Zhang et al., 2014; Glaze et al., 2015).
source: Previous theoretical accounts have postulated a shift in the starting point of the decision variables toward the bound of the previous choice (Yu and Cohen, 2008; Zhang et al., 2014; Glaze et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: The starting point bias assumption is based on the assumption that the representation of the decision variable decays slowly, leaving a trace of the observer's choice in the next trial (Cho et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2009; Gao et al., 2009; Bonaiuto et al., 2016).
source: This is based on the assumption that the representation of the decision variable decays slowly, leaving a trace of the observer's choice in the next trial (Cho et al., 2002; Gao et al., 2009; Gao et al., 2009; Bonaiuto et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Choice history biases might also originate from a slower (i.e. tens of seconds) across-trial accumulation of internal decision variables – analogous to the accumulation of external outcomes in value-based decisions (Sutton and Barto, 1998; Sugrue et al., 2004).
source: However, choice history biases might also originate from a slower (i.e. tens of seconds) across-trial accumulation of internal decision variables – analogous to the accumulation of external outcomes in value-based decisions (Sutton and Barto, 1998; Sugrue et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative mechanism, drawing on analogy to value-based decision-making.

claim: Previous experimental work on perceptual choice history biases either did not analyze the within-trial decision dynamics (Busse et al., 2011; de Lange et al., 2013; Akaishi et al., 2014; Fründ et al., 2014; Urai et al., 2017; Braun et al., 2018), or only tested for starting point biases, not accumulation biases (Cho et al., 2002; Gold et al., 2008; Yu and Cohen, 2008; Gao et al., 2009; Wilder et al., 2009; Bode et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014).
source: Previous experimental work on perceptual choice history biases either did not analyze the within-trial decision dynamics (Busse et al., 2011; de Lange et al., 2013; Akaishi et al., 2014; Fründ et al., 2014; Urai et al., 2017; Braun et al., 2018), or only tested for starting point biases, not accumulation biases (Cho et al., 2002; Gold et al., 2008; Yu and Cohen, 2008; Gao et al., 2009; Wilder et al., 2009; Bode et al., 2012; Jones et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research, identifying a gap in the literature.

claim: The DDM estimates model parameters from joint choices and RT distributions, and provides good fits to behavioral data from a large array of two-choice task (Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008).
source: The DDM estimates model parameters from joint choices and RT distributions, and provides good fits to behavioral data from a large array of two-choice task (Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous methodological work.

claim: A shift in starting point is most influential early in the decision process: it affects the leading edge of the RT distribution and shifts its mode.
source: A shift in starting point is most influential early in the decision process: it affects the leading edge of the RT distribution and shifts its mode.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the starting point bias mechanism, illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Starting point bias predicts that the majority of history-dependent choice biases occur on trials with fast RTs.
source: It predicts that the majority of history-dependent choice biases occur on trials with fast RTs (Figure 1c, green).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the starting point bias mechanism, illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: A drift bias is accumulated along with the evidence and therefore grows as a function of elapsed time.
source: A drift bias is instead accumulated along with the evidence and therefore grows as a function of elapsed time.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the drift bias mechanism.

claim: Drift bias strongly affects the trailing edge of the RT distribution with only a minor effect on the mode, altering choice fractions across the whole range of RTs.
source: Thus, drift bias strongly affects the trailing edge of the RT distribution with only a minor effect on the mode, altering choice fractions across the whole range of RTs (Figure 1c, blue).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the drift bias mechanism, illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: History-dependent changes in bound separation or mean drift rate may also occur, but they can only change overall RT and accuracy: those changes are by themselves not sufficient to bias the accumulation process toward one or the other bound, and thus toward choice repetition or alternation.
source: History-dependent changes in bound separation or mean drift rate may also occur, but they can only change overall RT and accuracy: those changes are by themselves not sufficient to bias the accumulation process toward one or the other bound, and thus toward choice repetition or alternation (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument about the limitations of other parameters in explaining choice history bias.

claim: Observers exhibited a wide range of idiosyncratic choice history biases across all experiments.
source: As found in previous work (Fründ et al., 2014; Abrahamyan et al., 2016; Urai et al., 2017), observers exhibited a wide range of idiosyncratic choice history biases across all experiments (Figure 2b,c).
evidence: This is an observation from the data, shown in Figure 2b,c, and consistent with previous research.

claim: The DDM fits matched several aspects of the behavioral data.
source: The DDM fits matched several aspects of the behavioral data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary of model validation results, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: RT distributions matched the model predictions reasonably well.
source: First, RT distributions matched the model predictions reasonably well (shown separately for each combination of stimuli and choices in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, darker colors indicate predicted RTs obtained through model simulations).
evidence: This is a model validation result, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Individual drift rate estimates correlated with individual perceptual sensitivity (d').
source: Third, individual drift rate estimates correlated with individual perceptual sensitivity (d', Figure 3—figure supplement 1a) and monotonically increased with stronger sensory evidence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a model validation result, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Individual drift rate estimates monotonically increased with stronger sensory evidence.
source: Third, individual drift rate estimates correlated with individual perceptual sensitivity (d', Figure 3—figure supplement 1a) and monotonically increased with stronger sensory evidence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a model validation result, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The success of the DDM in fitting fixed duration tasks was consistent with previous work (e.g. Ratcliff, 2006; Bode et al., 2012; Jahfari et al., 2012).
source: Yet, the success of the DDM in fitting these data was consistent with previous work (e.g. Ratcliff, 2006; Bode et al., 2012; Jahfari et al., 2012) and might have reflected the fact that observers set implicit decision bounds also when they do not control the stimulus duration (Kiani et al., 2008; but see Tsetsos et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Observers might set implicit decision bounds also when they do not control the stimulus duration (Kiani et al., 2008; but see Tsetsos et al., 2015).
source: Yet, the success of the DDM in fitting these data was consistent with previous work (e.g. Ratcliff, 2006; Bode et al., 2012; Jahfari et al., 2012) and might have reflected the fact that observers set implicit decision bounds also when they do not control the stimulus duration (Kiani et al., 2008; but see Tsetsos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the success of the DDM in fixed duration tasks, with citations to supporting and contrasting evidence.

claim: Models with history-dependent biases better explained the data than the baseline model without such history dependence.
source: Models with history-dependent biases better explained the data than the baseline model without such history dependence (Figure 3a), corroborating the observation that observers' behavior showed considerable dependence on previous choices (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is a model comparison result, shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The model with both history-dependent starting point and drift bias provided the best fit to five out of six datasets based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC; Akaike, 1974).
source: The model with both history-dependent starting point and drift bias provided the best fit to five out of six datasets (Figure 3a), based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC; Akaike, 1974 - note that we obtained the same results when instead using the hierarchical Deviance Information Criterion).
evidence: This is a model comparison result, shown in Figure 3a, using a standard statistical criterion.

claim: Consistent with a shift in drift bias, observers exhibited history-dependent choice biases across the entire range of RTs.
source: Consistent with a shift in drift bias, observers exhibited history-dependent choice biases across the entire range of RTs (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is an observation from the data, shown in Figure 3b, consistent with the drift bias mechanism.

claim: The biased choices on slow RTs could only be captured by models that included a history-dependent shift in drift bias.
source: In particular, the biased choices on slow RTs could only be captured by models that included a history-dependent shift in drift bias (Figure 3c, blue and dark green bars).
evidence: This is a model comparison result, shown in Figure 3c, demonstrating the necessity of drift bias to explain the data.

claim: The history shift in drift bias, but not the history shift in starting point, was robustly correlated to the individual probability of choice repetition.
source: The history shift in drift bias, but not the history shift in starting point, was robustly correlated to the individual probability of choice repetition (Figure 4a, significant correlations indicated with solid regression lines).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result, shown in Figure 4a, demonstrating the relationship between drift bias and choice repetition.

claim: The Bayes factor for the history shift in starting point approached zero, indicating strong evidence for the null hypothesis of no correlation.
source: Specifically, the Bayes factor for the history shift in starting point approached zero, indicating strong evidence for the null hypothesis of no correlation.
evidence: This is a Bayesian statistical result quantifying the evidence against a correlation.

claim: The Bayes factor for the history shift in drift indicated strong evidence for a correlation (Kass and Raftery, 1995).
source: The Bayes factor for the history shift in drift indicated strong evidence for a correlation (Kass and Raftery, 1995).
evidence: This is a Bayesian statistical result quantifying the evidence for a correlation, with citation to the interpretation criterion.

claim: The same qualitative pattern of results was obtained with an alternative fitting procedure (non-hierarchical G2 optimization).
source: The same qualitative pattern of results was obtained with an alternative fitting procedure (non-hierarchical G2 optimization, Figure 4—figure supplement 2a), as well as a model that allowed for additional across-trial variability in non-decision time (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is a robustness check showing that the results hold with different fitting methods.

claim: Letting non-decision time vary with each level of sensory evidence strength did not change the pattern of model comparison and correlation results.
source: Letting non-decision time vary with each level of sensory evidence strength (in the two datasets including multiple such levels) did not change the pattern of model comparison and correlation results (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is a robustness check showing that the results hold with additional model complexity.

claim: These findings are robust to specifics of the model and fitting method.
source: These findings are thus robust to specifics of the model and fitting method.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the robustness of the results, based on the various checks performed.

claim: The same effects were found for both drug groups as well as the placebo group in the Visual motion 2IFC #2 dataset.
source: The Visual motion 2IFC #2 also included pharmacological interventions in two sub-groups of participants (see Materials and methods); we found the same effects for both drug groups as well as the placebo group (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a robustness check showing that the results hold across different pharmacological conditions.

claim: A significant positive correlation between history shift in drift bias and P(repeat) was present for two sub-groups of participants, defined as 'repeaters' and 'alternators'.
source: A significant positive correlation between history shift in drift bias and P(repeat) was present for two sub-groups of participants, defined as 'repeaters' and 'alternators' (based on P(repeat) being larger or smaller than 0.5, respectively; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a subgroup analysis showing that the correlation holds for both types of participants.

claim: History shifts in starting point were mostly negative (a tendency toward choice alternation) across participants, regardless of their individual tendency toward choice repetition or alternation.
source: History shifts in starting point were mostly negative (a tendency toward choice alternation) across participants, regardless of their individual tendency toward choice repetition or alternation (Figure 4—figure supplement 5, significant in two out of six datasets).
evidence: This is an observation from the data, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The small but consistent negative effect on starting point likely explains why the formal model comparison favored a model with both history-dependent drift and starting point over one with only drift bias.
source: This small but consistent effect likely explains why our formal model comparison favored a model with both history-dependent drift and starting point over one with only drift bias (see also Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference about the model comparison results, based on the observed starting point effects.

claim: Only the history-dependent shift in drift bias accounted for individual differences in choice repetition.
source: Critically, only the history-dependent shift in drift bias accounted for individual differences in choice repetition (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding, shown in Figure 4.

claim: The same result holds in the two datasets without single-trial outcome feedback, implying that external feedback is not necessary for history shifts in drift bias.
source: First, the same result holds in the two datasets without single-trial outcome feedback (Figure 4a, bottom row), implying that external feedback is not necessary for history shifts in drift bias.
evidence: This is an observation from the data, shown in Figure 4a, demonstrating that feedback is not necessary for the effect.

claim: Individual repetition probability was best explained by history shifts in drift bias, not starting point, after both correct and error trials.
source: Across datasets, individual repetition probability was best explained by history shifts in drift bias, not starting point, after both correct (Figure 5b) and error (Figure 5c) trials.
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result, shown in Figures 5b and 5c, demonstrating the effect holds regardless of previous trial outcome.

claim: Even erroneous choices bias evidence accumulation on the next trial, in the same direction as correct choices.
source: Thus, even erroneous choices bias evidence accumulation on the next trial, in the same direction as correct choices.
evidence: This is an inference from the results showing similar effects after correct and error trials.

claim: Most participants were predominantly biased by their previous choice (95 'stay', 30 'switch'), while a third was biased by a combination of the previous choice and its correctness (26 'win-stay lose-switch', 42 'win-switch lose-stay').
source: Indeed, most participants were predominantly biased by their previous choice (95 'stay', 30 'switch'), while a third was biased by a combination of the previous choice and its correctness (26 'win-stay lose-switch', 42 'win-switch lose-stay'; Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the data, shown in Figure 2c.

claim: History-dependent drift biases did not require external feedback about choice outcome and were predominantly induced by the previous choice.
source: In sum, history-dependent drift biases did not require external feedback about choice outcome and were predominantly induced by the previous choice.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the analysis of correct vs. error trials.

claim: Choice history-dependent biases in evidence accumulation were accompanied by effects on drift rate and boundary separation.
source: These choice history-dependent biases in evidence accumulation were accompanied by effects on drift rate and boundary separation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), in line with previous work on post-error slowing (Dutilh et al., 2012; Goldfarb et al., 2012; Purcell and Kiani, 2016a).
evidence: This is an observation from the data, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, consistent with previous research.

claim: Inclusion of further lags improved the model's ability to account for the data, up to a lag of 2–4 after which model fits (ΔAIC) began to deteriorate.
source: Inclusion of further lags improved the model's ability to account for the data, up to a lag of 2–4 after which model fits (ΔAIC) began to deteriorate (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a model comparison result, shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In 4/6 datasets, the best-fitting model contained only history-dependent changes in drift, not starting point, over a scale of the previous 2–4 trials.
source: In 4/6 datasets, the best-fitting model contained only history-dependent changes in drift, not starting point, over a scale of the previous 2–4 trials.
evidence: This is a model comparison result from the multi-lag analysis.

claim: In two datasets, the best-fitting model was a hybrid where both drift and starting point varied as a function of choice history, up to two trials into the past.
source: In the other two datasets, the best-fitting model was a hybrid where both drift and starting point varied as a function of choice history, up to two to trials into the past (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a model comparison result from the multi-lag analysis.

claim: Previous choices shifted drift bias in line with individual history bias across several trials, whereas starting point did not consistently shift in the direction of history bias.
source: Previous choices shifted drift bias in line with individual history bias across several trials, whereas starting point did not consistently shift in the direction of history bias.
evidence: This is a summary of the history kernel analysis results.

claim: The effect of choice history on drift bias decayed over approximately three past trials, with a slower decay than for starting point.
source: The hybrid models showed that the effect of choice history on drift bias decayed over approximately three past trials (Figure 6a), with a slower decay than for starting point (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is an observation from the history kernel analysis, shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The regression weights for past trials (from lag two through each dataset's best-fitting lag) for drift bias – but not starting point - significantly correlated with the probability of repeating past choices at these same lags.
source: The regression weights for past trials (from lag two through each dataset's best-fitting lag) for drift bias – but not starting point - significantly correlated with the probability of repeating past choices at these same lags (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result from the multi-lag analysis, shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The biasing effect of choice history on evidence accumulation is long-lasting (longer than the effects on starting point), dependent on preceding choices several trials into the past, but independent of their correctness.
source: In sum, the biasing effect of choice history on evidence accumulation is long-lasting (longer than the effects on starting point), dependent on preceding choices several trials into the past, but independent of their correctness.
evidence: This is a summary of the multi-lag analysis results.

claim: The data were better explained by a history-dependent bias in the drift, rather than the starting point, in the Visual motion 2AFC (FD) dataset using motion energy estimates.
source: As expected (Figure 3a), the data were better explained by a history-dependent bias in the drift, rather than the starting point (Figure 7b1).
evidence: This is a model comparison result for the extended models, shown in Figure 7b1.

claim: Individual choice repetition probability was more strongly predicted by drift than starting point bias in the hybrid DDM model.
source: As in our previous analysis (Figure 4), individual choice repetition probability was more strongly predicted by drift than starting point bias (Figure 6c1).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result for the extended models, shown in Figure 7c1.

claim: A standard DDM with constant drift bias provided a better fit than DDMs with either a ramping drift bias, or a combination of constant and ramping drift bias.
source: In our data, a standard DDM with constant drift bias provided a better fit than DDMs with either a ramping drift bias, or a combination of constant and ramping drift bias (Figure 7b2).
evidence: This is a model comparison result for the extended models, shown in Figure 7b2.

claim: In the hybrid model with constant and ramping drift bias, the constant drift bias best predicted individual choice repetition behavior.
source: Furthermore, in the latter (hybrid) model, the constant drift bias best predicted individual choice repetition behavior (Figure 7c2), in line with the constant accumulation bias inferred from the standard DDM fits.
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result for the extended models, shown in Figure 7c2.

claim: Adding collapsing bounds substantially improved model fits, indicating the presence of a strong urgency signal in the Visual motion 2AFC (FD) task.
source: Indeed, adding collapsing bounds substantially improved our model fits (Figure 7b3). This indicates the presence of a strong urgency signal in this task, which had a relatively short stimulus presentation (750 ms) and a tight response deadline (1.25 s after stimulus offset).
evidence: This is a model comparison result for the extended models, shown in Figure 7b3, with inference about the task structure.

claim: A history-dependent drift bias best fit the data and captured individual choice repetition behavior also in the DDM with collapsing bounds.
source: Critically, a history-dependent drift bias best fit the data (Figure 7b3) and captured individual choice repetition behavior (Figure 7c3) also in the DDM with collapsing bounds.
evidence: This is a model comparison and correlation result for the extended models, shown in Figures 7b3 and 7c3.

claim: While there is evidence for collapsing bounds in the Visual motion 2AFC (FD) dataset, the conclusion about the impact of history bias on decision formation does not depend on its inclusion in the model.
source: In other words, while there is evidence for collapsing bounds in this dataset, our conclusion about the impact of history bias on decision formation does not depend on its inclusion in the model.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the robustness of the main conclusion.

claim: The leaky accumulator with biased accumulator input best explained the data, among all the models considered.
source: Critically, the leaky accumulator with biased accumulator input best explained the data, among all the models considered (Figure 7b4).
evidence: This is a model comparison result for the extended models, shown in Figure 7b4.

claim: The individually estimated input bias in the leaky accumulator model predicted individual choice repetition.
source: Furthermore, the individually estimated input bias predicted individual choice repetition (Figure 7c4).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result for the extended models, shown in Figure 7c4.

claim: Choice history might specifically bias the internal representation of sensory evidence feeding into the evidence accumulation process.
source: This suggests that choice history might specifically bias the internal representation of sensory evidence feeding into the evidence accumulation process.
evidence: This is an inference from the best-fitting leaky accumulator model with input bias.

claim: The effective bias accelerated in the best-fitting leaky accumulator model with collapsing bounds.
source: In this leaky accumulator (with collapsing bound), the effective bias accelerated (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation of the best-fitting model, shown in Figure 7d.

claim: The dynamics of the effective bias signal suggest that participants combined prior information with current evidence in a rational fashion.
source: Thus, the dynamics of the effective bias signal uncovered in Figure 7d suggest that participants combined prior information with current evidence in a rational fashion.
evidence: This is an inference from the effective bias dynamics, drawing on normative theory.

claim: Quantitative treatments of perceptual decision-making commonly attribute trial-to-trial variability of overt choices to noisy decision computations (Shadlen et al., 1996; Renart and Machens, 2014; Wyart and Koechlin, 2016).
source: Quantitative treatments of perceptual decision-making commonly attribute trial-to-trial variability of overt choices to noisy decision computations (Shadlen et al., 1996; Renart and Machens, 2014; Wyart and Koechlin, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Choice history explains trial-to-trial variability specifically in evidence accumulation, in a number of widely used perceptual choice tasks.
source: Our current results indicate that choice history explains trial-to-trial variability specifically in evidence accumulation, in a number of widely used perceptual choice tasks.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Ignoring trial-to-trial variations in evidence accumulation due to choice history will lead to an overestimation of the noise in the evidence accumulation process and resulting behavior.
source: Ignoring such trial-to-trial variations will lead to an overestimation of the noise in the evidence accumulation process and resulting behavior.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the findings for modeling practice.

claim: Individual differences in overt choice repetition behavior are explained by the degree to which choices bias the evidence accumulation, not the starting point, of subsequent decisions.
source: We here show that individual differences in overt choice repetition behavior are explained by the degree to which choices bias the evidence accumulation, not the starting point, of subsequent decisions.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: The accumulation bias is associated with choices made several trials into the past, and it grows steadily as the current decision unfolds.
source: This accumulation bias is associated with choices made several trials into the past, and it grows steadily as the current decision unfolds.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the multi-lag analysis and the effective bias dynamics.

claim: This insight calls for a revision of current models of choice history biases (Yu and Cohen, 2008; Zhang et al., 2014).
source: This insight calls for a revision of current models of choice history biases (Yu and Cohen, 2008; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings for theoretical models, with citations to previous work.

claim: Most previous studies with variations of evidence strength found an effect of asymmetric target probability on starting point shifts (Leite and Ratcliff, 2011; Mulder et al., 2012; White and Poldrack, 2014; Rorie et al., 2010; Gao et al., 2011; but only for decisions without time pressure, see Afacan-Seref et al., 2018).
source: Most of these studies explained the resulting behavioral biases in terms of starting point shifts (Leite and Ratcliff, 2011; Mulder et al., 2012; White and Poldrack, 2014; Rorie et al., 2010; Gao et al., 2011; but only for decisions without time pressure, see Afacan-Seref et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: One study with variations of evidence strength found an effect of asymmetric target probability on accumulation bias (Hanks et al., 2011) similar to the one identified in this study for choice history.
